Hannibal Hamlin was the first Vice President under Abraham Lincoln, serving from eighteen sixty-one to eighteen sixty-five. A Maine political stalwart representing the radical Republican faction's antislavery principles, Hamlin served as Vice President during the outbreak of the American Civil War and Lincoln's critical first term. As a link to the radical Republicans who demanded aggressive prosecution of the war, he held considerable influence over Republican war strategy. Before his vice presidency, Hamlin had served in the House of Representatives and as Governor of Maine, establishing himself as a stalwart of Maine Republican politics. He was also a newspaper editor and abolitionist whose passionate antislavery convictions aligned him with the party's core ideology. However, in eighteen sixty-four, Hamlin was not renominated for a second term. Lincoln, seeking a broader coalition, selected Tennessee War Democrat Andrew Johnson as his running mate instead. After leaving the vice presidency, Hamlin served in the U.S. Senate from Maine, becoming a leading voice for Reconstruction policy and equal rights for freed slaves. He supported the Radical Republican agenda of aggressive Reconstruction, placing him in conflict with President Andrew Johnson's more lenient approach to the South. Late in his career, Hamlin served as a customs house official in Maine and remained a respected elder statesman until his death in eighteen ninety-one.
